newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's Vranitzky says no new elections in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Austria's Vranitzky says no new elections in 1997.

text.p: Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky said on Wednesday in his New Year's address 1997 should be a year without new elections, appealing for calm in the country's troubled centre-left government coalition.
"The year that has just started should be one without nationwide elections," he said in his televised speech.

His comments came after an increasingly acrimonious row over selloff candidate Creditanstalt-Bankverein, which has put a strain on the coalition of Vranitzky's Social Democrats and their junior partner, the conservative People's Party.

"Despite the debate over the past days and weeks I am convinced that both government partners will stand by the coalition agreement and that we will put our reform course into action together," Vranitzky said.
Tension has been high since Bank Austria entered the fray for the sale of conservative stronghold Creditanstalt shortly before an original December 16 deadline for bids.

Bank Austria, effectively controlled by the Social Democrat-dominated City of Vienna, is up against rival offers from a consortium led by Austro-Italian insurer EA Generali, favoured by the conservatives, and Austrian entrepreneur Karl Wlaschek, an outsider.

Social Democrat Finance Minister Viktor Klima last week reopened the tender for the sale of the government's 70 percent stake in Austria's second biggest bank to give current bidders more time to improve their offers, setting a new deadline for January 10.
The conservatives want to see the bank floated on the Vienna bourse and said handing control of Creditanstalt to Bank Austria would be a breach of the coalition agreement.
The People's Party indicated it was ready to join forces with other parties to win the necessary majority in parliament against the Social Democrats, effectively threatening a government collapse.
The conservatives and the Social Democrats fell out in a budget row in October 1995, forcing a snap general election in December of the same year just 14 months after the last nationwide poll.
The two parties resumed their 10-year coalition partnership but relations have remained strained, particularly over economic policy.

Austrian President Thomas Klestil, still recovering from an acute bout of pneumonia that has confined him to hospital for several weeks in the autumn of last year, used his New Year's address to make a strong call for unity within the government.

"We have no time for arguments," Klestil said in his speech. "I have no sympathy for a political power game which threatens the cooperation within the government -- and I know how many of you think the same way."
